title: Sharding strategies
description: Learn different sharding strategies for horizontal scaling. Understand how to choose the right approach for your data distribution needs.

data.text: Sharding (horizontal partitioning) splits a large dataset across multiple database instances. Choosing the right sharding strategy is critical for balanced load distribution, query performance, and operational simplicity.
Apply a hash function to a shard key to determine which shard stores the data. This provides even distribution but makes range queries difficult.

items: Consistent hashing minimizes data movement when adding/removing shards
Even distribution of data across shards
Simple to implement and understand
Range queries require querying all shards
Hard to do aggregations across shards

data.title: Best For
data.text: User data, high-cardinality keys, lookup-heavy workloads. Not ideal for time-series data or analytical queries.
Partition data based on value ranges (e.g., A-M, N-Z for names; Jan-Mar, Apr-Jun for dates). Easy for range queries but can create hotspots.

items: Efficient range queries—only query relevant shards
Natural for time-series and ordered data
Risk of hotspots if data distribution is uneven
Rebalancing is complex when ranges grow unevenly
May require manual intervention for skew

data.title: Best For
data.text: Time-series data, logs, analytics, ordered datasets. Monitor for hotspots and be prepared to split ranges.
Maintain a lookup service (directory) that maps shard keys to shard locations. Flexible but adds an extra lookup step.

items: Most flexible—can change mapping without moving data
Easy to implement custom routing logic
Directory becomes a single point of failure
Extra network hop for each query
Directory must be highly available and scalable

data.title: Best For
data.text: Multi-tenant systems, geographic distribution, complex routing rules. Cache the directory mapping to reduce overhead.
Place data based on geographic location—users in Europe go to European shards. Improves latency but complicates global queries.

items: Low latency for local users
Compliance with data residency requirements
Global queries are slow and complex
Cross-region replication adds cost
Must handle data consistency across regions

data.text: The shard key is the most critical decision. It affects everything from performance to operational complexity.

items: High cardinality—many distinct values to distribute load
Even distribution—avoid hotspots in data or access patterns
Query alignment—most queries should filter on the shard key
Stability—key shouldn't change over time
Size considerations—key size affects index performance

data.title: Critical Decision
data.text: You can rarely change the shard key after sharding. Choose carefully—changing it requires massive data migration.

items: Rebalancing—moving data when adding/removing shards
Cross-shard transactions—hard to maintain ACID across shards
Joins across shards—expensive or impossible
Skewed workloads—some shards get more traffic
Operational complexity—managing many database instances

data.text: Don't shard too early. Replication and read replicas solve many problems.

items: When a single node can't store all your data
When write load exceeds a single node's capacity
When read replicas don't solve your performance issues
When you need to scale beyond vertical limits
When you have clear, stable shard keys
